title: Divergence-Free Neural Networks with Application to Image Denoising
claim: Relaxing noise assumptions forces estimators to lose expressivity; our constraint sits in a sweet spot, keeping more power while handling unknown, varying noise.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right spectrum arrow, ours highlighted with pink shading
description: A horizontal black arrow runs left to right, split by three vertical tick marks into four segments. Above the arrow each segment has a method name in black (SURE, UNSURE, CENSURE (ours), Noise2Self/Blind-spot nets). Under each name, in red, is the constraint on the estimator: unconstrained, expectation of the divergence equals nc, divergence equals nc for all y, and a per-coordinate partial-derivative constraint. The words 'Less expressive estimators' in red sit at the far right near the arrowhead. Below the arrow, black text gives the noise assumption for each segment: known sigma, unknown constant sigma, unknown non-constant sigma, and unknown non-constant sigma with applicability beyond Gaussian noise. The CENSURE segment has a light pink background, so the eye goes there first.
caption: Balancing expressive power in constraint-based self-supervised Gaussian denoising. When the noise model is fully specified, SURE yields the most expressive estimators, whose performance matches theoretically that of supervised methods. As assumptions on the noise are gradually relaxed, however, the learned estimators must reduce their expressivity to avoid overfitting the noise. In this work, we introduce divergence-constant estimators, a family that preserves much of the expressivity lost in blind-spot designs, yet still allows training even when the noise level σ is unknown and varies across the data.
abstract: We introduce a resource-efficient neural network architecture with zero divergence by design, adapted for high-dimensional problems. Our method is directly applicable to image denoising, for which divergence-free estimators are particularly well-suited for self-supervised learning, in accordance with Stein's unbiased risk estimation theory. Comparisons of our parameterization on popular denoising datasets demonstrate that it retains sufficient expressivity to remain competitive with other divergence-based approaches, while outperforming its counterparts when the noise level is unknown and varies across the training data.
